title: The unsafe command; goldens as theorems
objective: Add force move and give a successful call that leaves the invariant, find a call that separates a faulty evaluator from the goldens, and say which check catches a redefined evaluator.

blocks.md: Comparator checks your proof against a pinned statement. It is easy to hear that as "your semantics were checked".

choice.prompt: Comparator accepts your `step_preserves_inv` against the pinned statement. Is your evaluator right?

options.text: Yes: the statement is pinned, so the evaluator is too.
options.why: Pinning fixes the statement's text, not what your evaluator does.

options.text: Not established: the pin fixes the statement, not your evaluator.
options.why: Goldens are the check on the evaluator.

options.text: Yes, if only the standard axioms appear in the proof.
options.why: Axioms say what a proof trusts, not what a definition means.

blocks.md:
So far every command kept the invariant. Add one that does not: `force move n from x to y`, a move with no cover requirement, so R-cover has nothing to say about it. Admit it as well-typed and a successful step can leave `Inv`.

That ends `step_preserves_inv` for the extended language. The reference states its negation as `cex_force`, and `decide` closes it {{run:RUN-lean-unsafe-cmd}}. A counterexample the kernel checked settles the matter, so do not hunt for a cleverer proof. Keep the broken command in `broken/`, beside a fix that removes `force move` or demands a covering guard.
The unsafe command, called from an empty balance.
blocks.direction: The interpreter evaluates `Inv` on the outcome of a successful call and shows which part fails.

code.text:
command ForcePay(from, to, amount)
  do force move amount from from to to

start    mint 0 · a 0 · b 0
  ForcePay(a, b, 1)

call.prompt: Admit `force move` as well-typed. Can `step_preserves_inv` still be proved?

options.why: No proof exists once a kernel-checked counterexample does. Reading a violation as a proof difficulty is a mistake.
`cex_force` proves the negation by `decide`.
The counterexample settles it.

blocks.after: The call commits and leaves `a` at -1, so non-negativity fails while the total stays 0. Any amount above the balance does the same {{run:RUN-lean-unsafe-cmd}}.

choice.prompt: Every balance is 0. Which call to `ForcePay` makes a successful step that leaves `Inv`?

options.why: It debits `a` below zero with no cover. The class is any amount above the balance.
`Inv` exempts the mint, so debiting it leaves `Inv` intact.
Debit, then credit, on one account changes nothing.
A zero amount is rejected at the boundary, so no step succeeds.

blocks.md:
Comparator accepted your proof against the pinned statement. That checks the statement's text. The statement mentions your evaluator, `exec`, and you wrote it. Redefine `exec` to return `guardFailed` for every call and `step_preserves_inv` still holds, vacuously, because no call succeeds. Comparator checks against a challenge that copies your definitions, so it passes.

Goldens close the gap. A golden is a theorem, `theorem golden_k : exec p c s₀ = r := by decide`, whose right side comes from the reference. It is a theorem and not printed output because a closed `decide` proof adds no axiom, `native_decide` adds a `_native` one {{run:RUN-lean-axioms}}, and `#eval` can disagree with the kernel through `implemented_by` {{run:RUN-lean-implemented-by}}.
An evaluator redefined to reject every call, with one golden.
blocks.direction: The recorded receipt runs two checks on this source: comparator against the pinned statement, and the goldens.

code.text:
def exec (p : Program) (c : Call) (s : State) :
    Except Err (State × Output × List Effect) :=
  .error (.guardFailed c.name)

theorem golden_transfer_ok :
    exec refProgram transferCall s0 = .ok (s1, [], [.notify b]) := by
  decide

call.prompt: This evaluator returns `guardFailed` for every call. Which checks pass?

options.why: The statement matches and holds vacuously. The first golden that expects a commit evaluates to false.
A vacuous theorem does not make a golden true.
Comparator checks against the frozen challenge, which copied this evaluator.

blocks.after: The redefined evaluator passes comparator and fails the golden {{run:RUN-lean-golden-redef}}. The course makes the same kind of claim about the interpreter in this tab: that it agrees with the Lean reference on its goldens. That is a seam the course plants on itself, and it is tested the same way.

choice.prompt: A mutant evaluator computes both posting balances from the old state. Under the default policy, which call separates it from the goldens?

options.why: With two accounts the old and new state agree, so both evaluators return the same state.
The reference leaves `a` at 10. The mutant credits from the old balance and returns 15.
Both return `unknownAccount ghost` before any posting runs.
Both fail the guard before any posting runs.

choice.prompt: A mutant evaluator drops the account-existence check. Which call separates it from the goldens?

options.why: Both evaluators commit the same state.
The reference returns `unknownAccount ghost`. The mutant creates the missing recipient and commits.
Both commit an unchanged state.
Both fail the guard.

blocks.title: Production twin
blocks.md: Cedar tests its Rust implementation against its Lean model with differential random testing. In the paper, proofs found 4 bugs, and differential and property-based testing found 21 more (section 4, "Differential Random Testing", read 2026-10-23). LAB-3.10 and LAB-3.11 build that shape.

blocks.title: Reading
blocks.md: Read 2026-10-23. "How We Built Cedar", section 3 (the Lean model and its proofs) and section 4 (differential random testing). Optionally, Lean's "Validating Proofs" page.

blocks.title: Build this
blocks.md: Add `force move` to your semantics, watch `step_preserves_inv` fail, and keep the broken version in `broken/`. LAB-3.8 to LAB-3.11 then build the Rust side against the goldens.
